newsitem.title: FRANCE: States must privatise to create new Airbus - Dasa.
newsitem.headline: States must privatise to create new Airbus - Dasa.

text.p: European governments must give up some of their control and privatise state-owned firms in the Airbus aircraft consortium if Europe is to respond to U.S. competition, British and German executives said on Thursday.

The four partners in Airbus Industrie are struggling to find a compromise solution to converting the present partnership to a limited liability company by 1999, to boost competitiveness in the face of U.S. megamergers.

"This means for the first step of creating Airbus SCE (single corporate entity) that governments have to see the fundamental necessity of privatisation and, therefore, as shareholders, be willing to forego their influence," Wolfgang Piller, a member of the management board of Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG (Dasa) told a Financial Times conference.
European firms face a sharp escalation in competition with the planned merger of U.S. aircraft giants Boeing and McDonnell Douglas, and a linkup between defence firms Raytheon and Hughes.

Dasa and British Aerospace Plc (BAe) are both private companies and partners in Airbus. But the other senior partner, France's Aerospatiale, is state-owned and there is uncertainty whether the new Socialist government will go ahead with a privatisation planned by the previous administration.

"The process of privatisation is a prerequisite for any further steps in the consolidation of the European aerospace industry and demands some some very important actions by European governments," Piller said.
Aerospatiale was due to merge with private sector Dassault Aviation, as part of a consolidation of the French defence industry, and the new group would have been privatised by the end of this year.

The previous government planned to announce the merger terms at the Paris Le Bourget Air Show, starting June 14, but with the arrival of a Socialist administration hostile to state sell-offs, French executives are eagerly looking for statements on the fate of Aerospatiale and Dassault Aviation.

Dassault chairman Serge Dassault had made privatisation a condition for merging with the larger Aerospatiale. He said on Tuesday that a merger was "still on the agenda" after meeting Communist transport minister, Jean-Louis Gayssot.

Dasa's Piller said the creation of the new Airbus company "is a 'must' to reap the benefits of one integrated company, such as a common management structure and the ability to streamline operations to improve shareholder value".
Aerospatiale and Dasa each hold 38 percent of Airbus, while Bae has 20 percent and Construcciones Aeronauticas SA (CASA) of Spain, which is state-owned, has four percent.

Looking beyond integrating Airbus's civil activities, BAe executives pointed to the need to consolidate defence businesses by pooling national assets into a new European group, which would have an international shareholder base.
BAe chairman Mike Turner said that governments need to accept that self-dependency in the defence industry was not realistic and that surplus capacity needed to be taken out.

"Governments have a choice between relinquishing some of their control over their defence industry or watch them slowly die in the face of superior U.S. competition...every country will have to give something up," he said.
He added that different company valuations needed to be addressed in any merger of European aerospace and defence.
"I will be surprised if, when we arrive at the point of valuation in the merger process, all the major companies are valued at the same level," Turner said.
"We will need to reassure our shareholders that the value of our share in any new consolidated entity is no less than six billion pounds," he said, that amount being BAe's market capitalisation.
BAe's group managing director John Weston reiterated that the envisaged European company would "own all the assets, intellectual property and resources necessary to perform its business."
